title: Work
hookLine: work well, justly, and not endlessly
tomorrow: is money a blessing or a danger? Christians still argue it.

cards: Monday dread is practically its own genre: the alarm, the commute, the countdown to Friday. So here's an odd detail. In Genesis, work is not the punishment.
Before anything goes wrong in the story, before the fruit, before the hiding, God puts the man in the garden of Eden “to dress it and to keep it.” A job, in paradise.
And in the same chapter, a little earlier, God's own work comes to a stop. Why would a perfect garden need a gardener, and why would God need to stop?

teach.h: GOD ENDED HIS WORK, AND RESTED.
teach.b: Here's the solve. “And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.” In this picture, work is good, and it has an end.
The trouble comes later. Only after the disobedience does the ground bring thorns, and bread come in the sweat of the face.

teach.h: THE CURSE FALLS ON THE TOIL.
teach.b: The curse lands on the toil, not on the tending. So today's hook gives work three edges.

Work well: a garden is a real calling, and so is a classroom, a kitchen, a spreadsheet. Work justly: Jesus says “the labourer is worthy of his hire,” and James warns that wages “kept back by fraud” cry out.
A psalm says it bluntly: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.”
Working late every night isn't proof of faithfulness, and sleep is called a gift. That's the odd detail solved.
A gardener in paradise means work was made good. A God who stops means work was made to stop.

how: Some Christians speak of their work as a vocation, a calling; churches keep the Lord's day for worship and rest in different ways, and some Christians set a firm stopping time for work each day.

o: tending what's in your hands, well and fairly
a duty to keep going until it's all done
a punishment handed down for the first sin

games.q: the edges of work — tap the pairs.

s: in Genesis, work first appears as a punishment for sin
the man is put in the garden 'to dress it and to keep it' before anything goes wrong.
in Genesis, the curse falls on the ground, and toil turns to sweat
after the disobedience: thorns, and bread in the sweat of the face.
the psalm praises rising early and sitting up late
it calls that vain: he giveth his beloved sleep.

games.q: your manager texts at 9 p.m.: can you finish the report tonight? it isn't urgent; it's due friday. by the three edges, what fits?
o: say yes; a faithful worker never stops early.
reply in the morning, and do it well before friday.
ignore it for good; work has nothing to do with faith.
games.why: work well, work justly, and not endlessly: the report gets done well, and the night gets its rest.

practice: Name the time your work or study stops today. Name the one thing most likely to drag you past it, a last email, one more page, and decide now: when it shows up, I'll write it down for tomorrow and close the laptop.
If you pray, you can hand the unfinished pile to God for the night.

wordCard.voice: Work. Tending what's in your hands, done well and fairly, with a stopping point, the way God's own work had one.

orig.note: the Hebrew verb behind 'he rested' in Genesis 2:2: to stop, to cease.
